title: A prospectively validated law of structural lifespan

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a method that turns a short test, a nondestructive survey, or sparse inspection records into reliable predictions of how much load a structure will still carry decades later. Its defining achievement would be successful prediction of later measured outcomes on structures and exposure histories that were not used to tune the method. Prospective validation means publishing the predictions before those outcomes become available.

The intended scope includes deterioration and deformation caused by interacting corrosion, creep, shrinkage, and fatigue. A useful prediction would state remaining flexural or shear capacity and, where deformation governs usability or safety, the relevant time-dependent deformation. Reinforced concrete is the clearest starting domain in the supplied research; extension to steel structures and to every listed combination of mechanisms remains an ambition requiring separate evidence.

Conceptual distinction: remaining capacity at a future date is different from remaining lifespan. A lifespan prediction must specify the threshold that ends acceptable service, along with assumptions about future loading, exposure, and maintenance. The word “law” expresses the ambition for a transferable predictive framework within a declared domain. A collection of curves fitted to past observations would not, by itself, establish that capability.

significance.text: Conditional assessment: independently validated predictions of decade-scale remaining capacity, with uncertainty narrow enough to support engineering decisions, would make deterioration much more calculable. Engineers could compare repair strategies by their expected effect on future capacity, assess whether continued service is justified, and make better quantified commitments about design life. The advance would be especially consequential if it transferred across materially different structures, exposures, and interacting deterioration mechanisms.

These benefits would depend on more than small average prediction errors. Design-life commitments require calibrated uncertainty and explicit operating conditions. Reducing unexpected failures also requires coverage of the failure modes that matter, appropriate inspection and maintenance, and effective use of the predictions. A correct capacity forecast under one loading and exposure scenario cannot guarantee safety after those conditions change.

The comparison with calculus conveys the ambition of a general language for structural change over time; it is an evaluative analogy, not an established measure of impact. Feasibility remains uncertain. The method would not itself create a material capable of lasting longer, and a sensor system that warns of collapse weeks ahead would demonstrate a different, shorter-horizon capability. Strong performance on several structures could establish an important initial result without establishing a broadly general lifespan law.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is defensible extrapolation from short or sparse observations to decade-scale structural performance under declared future conditions. The supplied research attributes to Akiyama, Frangopol, and Xu an account of uncertainty that varies across space and time, including difficulty inferring quantities such as remaining reinforcement area from inspection and monitoring. Those reported observations explain why measurements of visible condition do not straightforwardly determine future load capacity. The source text was not retained, so the attribution cannot be independently checked from the supplied materials.

Engineering synthesis: a central barrier is an inverse problem—different hidden damage states can be consistent with similar surface observations or short-test results. A successful method would need to identify which internal states matter for future capacity, connect those states to structural behavior, and carry measurement uncertainty through to its predictions. It must also address interactions among mechanisms rather than assuming that separately calibrated corrosion, creep, shrinkage, and fatigue estimates automatically combine correctly.

Transfer beyond calibration conditions is another barrier. The supplied research reports that Qi and colleagues discuss limitations in model data requirements and accuracy, including bias when environmental factors differ from assumed conditions. This reported concern supports the need to test unfamiliar exposure histories, but the review text is unavailable in the supplied evidence. It does not establish that every empirical model fails under changed exposure or that a mechanism-based model would necessarily succeed.

Engineering synthesis: long-horizon validation is itself difficult. Later capacity must be measured convincingly, future loading and maintenance must be documented, and accelerated tests must have a justified relationship to natural exposure if they are used. The method must distinguish uncertainty about the structure's present condition from uncertainty about its future environment and model behavior. Otherwise, apparent precision could conceal assumptions that dominate the lifespan estimate.

current_state.text: The supplied bibliography identifies Akiyama, Frangopol, and Xu's “Probabilistic service life assessment of corroded concrete structures: a state-of-the-art review,” reported as published online on 31 January 2025 in Structure and Infrastructure Engineering, volume 21, issues 7–8, pages 1081–1100. The research summary describes Bayesian updating, stochastic simulation, and learning methods as active tools and reports that prediction of performance and remaining service life from inspection and monitoring remains challenging. These are reported components of a research program, rather than a documented demonstration of the proposed prospectively validated law.

The research records abstract-only access to Akiyama and colleagues. No retained abstract or full text accompanies the source index, so that access scope and the detailed method descriptions cannot be independently verified here. The publication concerns corroded concrete structures; its bibliographic scope alone cannot establish results for steel structures or for all combinations of corrosion, creep, shrinkage, and fatigue.

The bibliography also identifies Qi, Peng, Yang, Xia, and Xu's “Review of Research on Prediction Models for Residual Life of Concrete Structures,” reported as published on 7 June 2025 in Coatings, volume 15, article 693. The supplied research describes its coverage as physical, empirical, statistical, and machine-learning life models, with continuing limitations in data requirements and accuracy. No retained source text is supplied, so these descriptions remain attributed reports rather than independently checked findings.

The supplied materials contain no documented prospective demonstration of decade-scale capacity prediction meeting the proposed criteria. They also contain no search evidence sufficient to establish whether the capability remained open as of 1 November 2026. This evidence gap does not show that the cited reviews are wrong or that no relevant achievement exists. Figures of less than 3 percent error and prediction beyond 200 years have no supplied primary-source support and are not treated as demonstrated performance; the earlier claim that a primary-source search failed to find them cannot be verified either.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: publish and register predictions before follow-up for several in-service structures or a long-duration natural-exposure series withheld from model tuning. Use only information available at the prediction date. Predict remaining flexural or shear capacity at specified future horizons, together with time-dependent deformation wherever it governs performance, and compare those predictions with later measured outcomes.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered remaining-capacity predictions are compared with later measured outcomes

completion_criteria.text: Proposed protocol: declare the intended structural and material domain, relevant deterioration mechanisms, prediction horizons, future loading and exposure assumptions, and maintenance conditions in advance. Define the measured outcomes, measurement uncertainty, error calculation, and acceptance rules before seeing the results. A claim about lifespan must additionally define the failure or serviceability threshold whose crossing ends acceptable service.
completion_criteria.label: Evaluation conditions and lifespan-ending thresholds are defined in advance

completion_criteria.text: A capacity-error band on the order of 10–20 percent is a proposed starting criterion, not an established standard or a verified equivalent of ordinary strength-calculation tolerances. Its suitability would depend on the decision being supported and the consequences of overprediction. Assessment should examine systematic bias, large errors, and uncertainty coverage as well as aggregate accuracy. Refitting a chloride model, creep formula, or fatigue S–N relationship to the evaluation outcomes would not satisfy the prospective test.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective capacity-error assessment examines accuracy, bias, and uncertainty coverage

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and breadth requirements: make the prediction procedure, parameter choices, available inputs, and outcome measurements sufficiently accessible for independent teams to reproduce the assessment and test new cases. Validation should expand across the materials, structures, exposures, and mechanism interactions claimed by the method. Passing finite tests establishes demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality. Initial results on corroded concrete would leave broader steel and coupled-mechanism claims to subsequent validation.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction and expanded validation establish demonstrated breadth

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: STR-01, “Flaw-tolerant bulk members at near-theoretical specific strength,” concerns the strength and defect tolerance of members; STR-03, “A cast mineral solid that can be a complete primary structure,” concerns a material's structural role. STR-09 could assess how their capacity changes with time, but predictive success would not establish either material breakthrough. Conversely, high initial strength or structural completeness would not establish predictable lifespan.

Roster-based synthesis: STR-02, “Repeated autonomous restoration of full structural capacity,” STR-05, “Primary members whose mechanical state can be reprogrammed in service,” and STR-06, “Load-bearing structures that grow and remodel,” concern structures that actively change their condition or properties. A lifespan prediction for such systems would need explicit assumptions about restoration, reprogramming, growth, or remodeling. Predicting those changes and producing them are distinct capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis: STR-04, “Field-scale broadband seismic cloaking,” STR-10, “Ordinary buildings that remain undamaged and usable after design-level earthquakes,” and STR-11, “Passive damping that removes resonant amplification from governing modes,” concern response to dynamic loading. Their performance could affect future damage and therefore enter STR-09's loading and deterioration assumptions. Long-term capacity prediction would not itself demonstrate seismic cloaking, undamaged earthquake performance, or removal of resonant amplification.

Roster-based synthesis: STR-07, “Topological control that denies an undesigned collapse mechanism,” and STR-12, “Disproportionate collapse made unavailable after loss of any one primary member,” concern which collapse paths a structure permits. They overlap with STR-09 through failure-mode coverage: an accurate forecast of one member's capacity cannot by itself establish system-level resistance to collapse. Preventing specified collapse mechanisms likewise does not determine the time remaining before other serviceability or capacity limits are reached.

Roster-based synthesis: STR-08, “Primary structure that stores the host system's useful energy,” combines structural and energy-storage functions. Applying STR-09 to it would require a declared account of how operating conditions and degradation affect load-bearing capacity and, if claimed, useful energy storage. Structural lifespan and energy-storage performance would remain separate outcomes to validate.

change_log.change: Preserved STR-09's identity and prospective-validation requirement while defining capacity prediction separately from lifespan prediction.
change_log.reason: A lifespan claim requires a specified end-of-service threshold and assumptions about future loading, exposure, and maintenance.

change_log.change: Integrated the research's mechanism detail with the review's distinctions about hidden condition, extrapolation, uncertainty, and validation breadth.
change_log.reason: These distinctions explain the scientific challenge without treating the hypothetical capability as achieved.

change_log.change: Retained reported findings from both 2025 reviews with explicit attribution and access limitations.
change_log.reason: The research contains useful explanatory detail, but no retained source texts permit independent verification of those accounts.

change_log.change: Qualified applicability to steel and to all listed interacting mechanisms.
change_log.reason: The supplied reviews concern concrete, and their bibliographic records do not establish the full intended domain.

change_log.change: Recast warranted lifespans and fewer unexpected failures as conditional consequences.
change_log.reason: Those outcomes require calibrated uncertainty, relevant failure-mode coverage, stated operating conditions, and effective implementation.

change_log.change: Retained the proposed 10–20 percent capacity-error band while removing its asserted equivalence to ordinary calculation tolerances.
change_log.reason: The numerical band is a proposal; the comparison lacks supplied support.

change_log.change: Expanded completion criteria to cover preregistration, measurement uncertainty, reproducibility, and domain-specific validation.
change_log.reason: Several successful predictions could demonstrate an initial capability without establishing a general law.

change_log.change: Excluded less-than-3-percent error and 200-plus-year prediction from demonstrated performance, and removed the claim that a primary-source search had ruled them out.
change_log.reason: Neither the numerical assertions nor the reported search conclusion can be verified from the supplied evidence.

change_log.change: Added distinctions and overlaps for every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: The related innovations can affect structural lifespan or its prediction while remaining separate capabilities.

unresolved_issues: The cited reviews' contents and detailed attributions remain unverified because no retained abstracts or full texts were supplied.
The research's reported abstract-only access to Akiyama and colleagues cannot be independently confirmed.
The supplied evidence does not establish the field's state as of 1 November 2026 or identify a qualifying prospective demonstration.
The intended domain still needs precise boundaries for materials, structural types, deterioration mechanisms, exposure conditions, and prediction horizons.
A lifespan formulation needs an explicit end-of-service threshold and a treatment of uncertain future loading, exposure, and maintenance.
The feasibility and decision usefulness of the proposed 10–20 percent capacity-error band remain open; it is not an established acceptance standard.
A practical protocol for later capacity measurement, independent replication, and justified use of accelerated exposure remains to be specified.
The origins and validity of the less-than-3-percent and 200-plus-year figures remain unresolved; lack of supplied support does not establish that they are false.
